title: Modal Verbs and Semi-modals

toc.title: 24.2 Ability: can, could, be able to
24.6 Past forms of modals and what they criticise

html:
A modal verb is a helping verb that does not describe an action but colours it: it says whether the action is possible, permitted, necessary, advisable or likely. The nine pure modals are can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should and must. NEB Q7 tests them in three ways — choose the right modal for a stated function, rewrite a sentence with a modal of the same meaning (It is necessary for you to go → You must go), or correct a sentence in which the modal is followed by the wrong verb form.

Four grammar rules that apply to every pure modal
  1. A modal is followed by the bare infinitive — V1 with no to: She can swim**, never ~~can to swim~~ or ~~can swims~~.
  2. A modal never takes -s in the third person: He must go.
  3. A modal makes its own question and negative with no do: Can you come? He cannot come. Never ~~Do you can come?~~
  4. Two modals cannot stand together: ~~He will can do it~~ → He will be able to do it.

24.1 The complete modal table

Modal Function Example Negative
can present ability She can speak four languages. cannot / can't
can informal permission Can I borrow your notes? can't (= not allowed)
can general possibility Landslides can block the Prithvi Highway. can't (= impossible)
could past ability At five he could already read. couldn't
could polite request / suggestion Could you pass the file? couldn't
could present possibility (weak) He could be at the library. couldn't (= impossible)
may formal permission May I come in, sir? may not
may possibility (about 50 %) It may rain in the afternoon. may not
may wish, blessing May you live long! —
might weaker possibility (about 30 %) She might join us later. might not
might very polite request Might I make a suggestion? —
will future, prediction, promise I will return the book tomorrow. will not / won't
will willingness, request Will you help me carry this? won't (= refuses)
will present habit / characteristic Boys will be boys. —
would polite request / offer Would you like some tea? wouldn't
would past habit We would go to the river every Saturday. wouldn't
would unreal / conditional result If I had money, I would buy it. wouldn't
shall offer or suggestion with I/we Shall we start? shan't
shall formal obligation in rules The tenant shall pay by the 5th. shall not
should advice, mild obligation You should see a doctor. should not
should expectation The parcel should arrive today. shouldn't
must strong obligation from the speaker You must submit it by Friday. must not (prohibition)
must logical certainty The lights are on — she must be at home. can't (= certainly not)

24.2 Ability: can, could, be able to

  • can — present or general ability: Nirmala can ride a motorbike.
  • could — general ability in the past: My grandfather could walk from Ilam to Fikkal in three hours.
  • was/were able to — a single successful act in the past ("managed to"). The fire was spreading, but the neighbours were able to rescue the goats. (could is wrong here, because it means general ability, not one success.)
  • be able to supplies the forms a modal cannot make: will be able to, have been able to, to be able to.
Two modals in a row

English allows only one modal in a verb phrase. ~~She will can join us.~~ → She will be able to join us. ~~He must can finish it.~~ → He must be able to finish it. ~~You should must apologise.~~ → You must apologise / You should apologise.

24.3 Permission, requests, offers and suggestions

Function Least formal → most formal Example
Asking permission can → could → may → might May I leave early today, madam?
Giving permission can, may You may use the library after four.
Refusing permission cannot, may not, must not Visitors may not enter the ward.
Request will → can → could → would Could you lend me Rs 200?
Offer shall, can, would like Shall I carry your bag?
Suggestion shall we, could, why don't we Shall we visit Swayambhu on Saturday?
Invitation would like Would you like to join us for tea?

Answering a request or permission question keeps the same modal where possible: "May I sit here?" — "Yes, you may." / "Could you help me?" — "Yes, of course." Do not answer Could you…? with Yes, I could; that sounds like a comment on your ability, not an agreement.

24.4 Obligation, necessity and their negatives

Form Meaning Example
must obligation the speaker imposes; also an internal duty You must wear a helmet.
have to / has to obligation from outside — a rule, a law, circumstances Passengers have to show a ticket.
had to past obligation (there is no past of must) We had to walk because of the strike.
will have to future obligation You will have to repeat the test.
should / ought to advice, what is right You should revise every day.
had better strong advice, with a warning of a bad result You had better leave now, or you will miss the bus.
need to necessity I need to renew my licence.
be supposed to expected by a rule or arrangement We are supposed to be there by nine.

The negatives carry completely different meanings. This is the single most examined point in the unit.

Negative Meaning Example
must not / mustn't prohibition — it is forbidden You mustn't touch the wires.
do not have to / don't have to no obligation — it is not necessary It is Saturday, so you don't have to get up early.
need not / needn't no obligation (same as don't have to) You needn't bring your own lunch.
should not advice against You shouldn't eat so late.
cannot / can't inability, or "certainly not true" He can't be in Nepalgunj; I saw him an hour ago.

*mustn't* is not the negative of *must*

The opposite of You must go is You don't have to go (it is not necessary), not You mustn't go (you are forbidden to go). Q7 items often ask you to rewrite It is not necessary for you to come — the answer is You needn't come or You don't have to come, never ~~You mustn't come~~.

*had better* has no *to*, and *ought* keeps its *to*

~~You had better to go now.~~ → You had better go now. ~~You ought go now.~~ → You ought to go now. Also note had better refers to the present or future, not the past, in spite of the word had.

24.5 Degrees of certainty — deduction

When a modal expresses how sure the speaker is, the whole set forms a scale.

The same scale in the past puts have + V3 after the modal:

Present deduction Past deduction Meaning
He must be ill. He must have been ill. I am sure it was so.
She may be at home. She may have been at home. Perhaps it was so.
They might know. They might have known. Perhaps, less likely.
It can't be true. It can't have been true. I am sure it was not so.

24.6 Past forms of modals and what they criticise

Form Meaning Example
should have + V3 the right thing was not done — regret or criticism You should have told me earlier.
shouldn't have + V3 a wrong thing was done She shouldn't have shouted at the porter.
ought to have + V3 same as should have He ought to have checked the ticket.
could have + V3 it was possible but did not happen We could have caught the earlier bus.
needn't have + V3 it was done, but it was unnecessary You needn't have paid; entry was free.
didn't need to + V1 it was unnecessary, so it was not done I didn't need to buy a ticket, so I walked in.
would have + V3 an unreal past result I would have come if you had called.
must have + V3 a confident conclusion about the past The road must have been blocked.
*needn't have done* versus *didn't need to do*

You needn't have waited — you did wait, and it turned out to be unnecessary. You **didn't need to wait — it was unnecessary, and (normally) you did not wait. The two are not interchangeable, and NEB has set this contrast in Q7.

24.7 Semi-modals

Semi-modals behave partly like modals in meaning but like ordinary verbs in grammar: they change for tense and person, and they need do for questions and negatives.

Semi-modal Meaning Note
be able to ability supplies the missing forms of can
have to / have got to outside obligation changes tense: had to, will have to
need to necessity Does he need to come?
used to + V1 a discontinued past habit or past state I used to cycle to school. Question: Did you use to…?
be going to + V1 intention, or prediction from evidence She is going to apply for the scholarship.
be about to + V1 on the point of The programme is about to begin.
had better + V1 strong advice no to, no tense change
would rather + V1 preference I would rather walk than wait.
be supposed to expected by rule or plan You are supposed to wear the uniform.
dare / need can be modal or ordinary verb He dare not speak / He doesn't dare to speak.
*used to* versus *be used to*

used to + V1 = a past habit that has stopped: *I used to drink milk tea. be/get used to + V-ing / noun = be accustomed to: I am used to drinking black tea now. The second one keeps the -ing*, and it can be in any tense.

Recognising the function the question wants

Q7 modal items almost always name the function in brackets or in the instruction: (obligation), (possibility), (prohibition), (advice), (past ability), (request). Match the label to the modal before you write anything: obligation → must/have to; prohibition → mustn't; no obligation → needn't; advice → should/ought to/had better; possibility → may/might/could; certainty → must; impossibility → can't; past ability → could; one past success → was able to.

Worked transformation 24.1 — a rewrite with the same meaning

Problem. Rewrite using a modal: It is not necessary for you to attend the Saturday class.

Solution — step by step.

  1. Name the function. "It is not necessary" = absence of obligation.
  2. Pick the modal for that function. Absence of obligation is needn't or don't have to. It is not mustn't, which would mean the class is forbidden.
  3. Fit the subject and the bare infinitive. you + needn't + attend.

Answer. You needn't attend the Saturday class. (Also correct: You don't have to attend the Saturday class.)

Worked transformation 24.2 — a deduction about the past

Problem. Express as a deduction: I am sure Anita did not take the bus, because her bicycle is missing.

Solution — step by step.

  1. Is the statement positive or negative? Negative — "did not take".
  2. How sure is the speaker? Completely sure. On the certainty scale, "certain it is NOT true" is can't.
  3. Is the event past? Yes, so add have + V3 after the modal: can't have taken.
  4. Assemble.

Answer. Anita can't have taken the bus, because her bicycle is missing.

Writing mustn't have taken is wrong: mustn't means prohibition, never negative deduction.

Worked transformation 24.3 — correcting a modal error

Problem. Correct: When he was young he can run very fast, but now he will not can run at all because he had better to rest his knee.

Solution — step by step.

  1. he can run in a past sentence. The time is past and the meaning is general ability → could run.
  2. will not can run. Two modals cannot stand together. Replace the second with the semi-modal → will not be able to run.
  3. had better to rest. Had better takes the bare infinitive → had better rest.

Answer. When he was young he could run very fast, but now he will not be able to run at all because he had better rest his knee.

Chapter summary

  • A modal takes the bare infinitive, never adds -s, needs no do for questions and negatives, and cannot be joined to another modal.
  • Ability: can (now), could (past, general), was/were able to (one past success), be able to (all other forms).
  • Permission rises in formality: can → could → may → might.
  • Obligation: must (from the speaker), have to (from outside), had to (past), should / ought to / had better (advice).
  • mustn't = forbidden; needn't and don't have to = not necessary. They are opposites, not synonyms.
  • Certainty scale: must (sure it is) > will > should > may > might/could

    may not > can't (sure it is not).

  • For the past, add have + V3: must have gone, might have gone, can't have gone.
  • should have + V3 criticises what was not done; needn't have + V3 says something done was unnecessary.
  • Semi-modals — be able to, have to, need to, used to, be going to, had better, would rather, be supposed to — carry modal meanings but behave like ordinary verbs.

Practice questions

Fill in the blanks with a suitable modal verb (1 mark each)

  1. ____ you please open the window? It is very hot in here. (polite request) [1]
  2. Students ____ not use mobile phones during the examination. (prohibition) [1]
  3. You ____ see a doctor if the fever does not come down. (advice) [1]
  4. My grandmother ____ read without spectacles even at eighty. (past ability) [1]
  5. It is a holiday tomorrow, so we ____ get up early. (absence of obligation) [1]
  6. Take an umbrella; it ____ rain in the afternoon. (possibility) [1]
  7. His bike is at the gate, so he ____ be at home. (certainty) [1]
  8. ____ I use your dictionary for a moment, sir? (formal permission) [1]
Answers

1. Could (or Would) — the polite request forms.

2. must — must not expresses prohibition.

3. should (or ought to) — advice.

4. could — general ability in the past.

5. needn't (or don't have to) — no obligation, not prohibition.

6. may (or might) — a possibility about the future.

7. must — a confident conclusion from evidence.

8. May (or Might) — the formal permission form.

Rewrite the sentences as instructed (1 mark each)

  1. It is necessary for you to renew your licence. — Rewrite with have to. [1]
  2. Smoking is forbidden inside the hospital. — Rewrite with must. [1]
  3. Perhaps she is waiting at the bus park. — Rewrite with may. [1]
  4. I am sure he has forgotten the meeting. — Rewrite with must. [1]
  5. It was a mistake to lend him the money. — Rewrite with shouldn't. [1]
  6. He managed to swim across the Karnali in spite of the current. — Rewrite with able to. [1]
  7. I cycled to school every day when I was a child. — Rewrite with used to. [1]
  8. Why don't we go to Godawari on Saturday? — Rewrite with shall. [1]
Answers

9. You have to renew your licence. — outside necessity.

10. You must not smoke inside the hospital. — mustn't is prohibition.

11. She may be waiting at the bus park. — may + bare infinitive for possibility.

12. He must have forgotten the meeting. — certainty about a past event.

13. I shouldn't have lent him the money. — criticism of a past action.

14. He was able to swim across the Karnali … — one successful past act.

15. I used to cycle to school every day … — a discontinued past habit.

16. Shall we go to Godawari on Saturday? — shall makes a suggestion with we.

Correct the errors in the following sentences (1 mark each)

  1. She can to speak Maithili and Bhojpuri fluently. [1]
  2. He must goes to Kathmandu for the interview. [1]
  3. Do you can help me with this sum? [1]
  4. Next year I will can drive a car. [1]
  5. You had better to consult your class teacher. [1]
  6. You mustn't come to the picnic if you are busy; it is not compulsory. [1]
  7. He ought go home before it gets dark. [1]
  8. I am used to get up at five every morning these days. [1]
  9. She mustn't have taken my umbrella; she was not even here. [1]
  10. We could rescue the calf from the flooded field yesterday. [1]
Answers

17. She can speak … — a modal takes the bare infinitive, with no to.

18. He must go … — a modal is never followed by an -s form.

19. Can you help me …? — modals form questions without do.

20. Next year I will be able to drive a car. — two modals cannot stand together.

21. You had better consult … — had better takes no to.

22. You needn't come to the picnic … — absence of obligation, not prohibition.

23. He ought to go home … — ought keeps its to.

24. I am used to getting up at five … — be used to is followed by -ing.

25. She can't have taken my umbrella … — negative deduction uses can't have.

26. We were able to rescue the calf … — one successful past act, not general ability.
